chapter_theme: Poems 121 to 140 are praise of three chiefs as givers: Malaiyaman Kari of Mullur (121 to 126), Ay Andiran of Pothiyil (127 to 136, 138) and the lord of Nanjil (137, 139, 140). They test what good giving is: judging rank, giving sober, giving without hope of a next-world return, and giving beyond what was asked.

121.reading: Bards come from all four directions with one man in mind, so giving much is easy but knowing each one's due rank is hard; if the great giver understands this, he should stop looking at all poets with one undiscriminating eye.
121.nuance: Kapilar praises Kari by correcting him: the fault named is not meanness but indiscriminate giving, so generosity is assumed and judgment is what is asked. The poet's own interest is plain, since a poet of standing is the one who loses when all are treated alike.

thinai_evidence.note: counsel addressed to a named patron about how he gives, which is admonition (செவியறிவுறூஉ) under praise rather than a general truth

122.reading: Kari's land cannot be taken by the sea and enemies dare not attack it, yet it belongs to the fire-tending brahmins; the tribute the three crowned kings send him to win his help belongs to the bards who praise his clan; nothing is his own but the shoulders of his wife, chaste as the northern star, and still he holds himself proud.
122.nuance: The poem lists Kari's possessions only to give each away, so the praise is an inventory of dispossession. The one thing kept is his wife, set apart by her chastity; the closing word பெருமிதம் makes pride rest on what he has given, not what he holds.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron whose land and revenue are said to belong to brahmins and bards

123.reading: Anyone who drinks the morning's toddy and grows merry finds it easy to give away chariots, but the jewelled chariots that Malayan of unfading fame gave while sober outnumber the raindrops that fall on the heights of fertile Mullur.
123.nuance: The measure of the gift is not its size but the giver's state: a drunk man's chariot costs him nothing in judgment, a sober man's is chosen. The rain on Mullur, his own hill, makes the gifts as natural to the land as its weather.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron's sober giving

124.reading: Those who sing Malayan of the mountain of loud waterfalls never go home empty-handed, even if they set out on an unlucky day, are held back by bad omens of birds, arrive at the wrong hour and speak without skill.
124.nuance: Every rule a suppliant was meant to keep (the right day, good omens, timing, skilful speech) is listed only to be cancelled by the patron's nature, so the poem praises him by making the bard's craft unnecessary.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron from whom no singer returns empty

125.reading: The bard will feast on fat roast meat and drink by turns in Malayan's hall, where the toddy he relishes like nectar is a reward earned as the ploughing ox earns its straw; in the battle between two kings, the victor says Malayan made him win and the loser says that without Malayan victory would have been easy, so the strong hero of the high hill is the one man both sides name.
125.nuance: The praise is built from the testimony of both enemies: Malayan fought as an ally, and his worth is proven by the loser's complaint as much as by the winner's thanks. The ox simile turns the patron's drinking into wages for war-work, not indulgence.

thinai_evidence.note: the excellence of a warrior chief proven in battle on another king's side

comparisons.tenor: the white fat pieces of roast meat
Malayan drinking his toddy after the labour of war
Malayan, the hero of the high hill

126.reading: Descendant of the hero who crowned bards with gold lotuses taken from enemy elephants' brow-plates, we are not skilled singers, yet poverty drove us to you: since Kapilar, the flawless brahmin, sang your fame so fully that no room is left for those who come asking, we are like other boats that cannot sail the sea lane the Chera's gold-laden ships have cut; lord of the land of palmyra groves who holds back hostile kings in battle.
126.nuance: A later poet admits he follows a master: Kapilar's praise has filled the space, and the ship simile makes poetic praise a trade route already taken. The modesty is itself a bid, since the bard binds himself to Kari's generosity rather than to his own skill.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard asking a patron for a gift

comparisons.vehicle: பொலந்தரு நாவாய் ஓட்டிய அவ் வழிப் பிறகலம் செல்கலாது
comparisons.tenor: the later bards after Kapilar's praise
the roar of the war drum

127.reading: They say Ay's palace stands bare, since bards have led away its elephants and the forest peacocks flock to the empty tethering posts, with only its women left wearing the jewel that cannot be given; yet it is not like the cities of drum-owning kings who fill their own bellies with savoury food, give none away and lose their fame.
127.nuance: Poverty here is the proof of wealth: the emptied hall is set against the full but famous-less cities. The one thing not given, the women's jewel, is the marriage token, so the line marks the limit of a king's giving without saying so.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron whose giving has emptied his palace

comparisons.tenor: the black horn of the small lute

128.reading: On Ay's cloud-wrapped Pothiyil, a female monkey on a branch of the jackfruit tree in the common ground beats the taut face of a drum the bards hung there, taking it for fruit, and the swan rises in answer and dances; only a dancing woman may approach that hill, and proud kings can hardly come near it.
128.nuance: The hill is open and closed at once: performers' drums hang in its common ground and a dancer may walk in, but kings cannot. The comic scene of the monkey and the swan shows a place so full of the bards' music that even the animals play it.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron's hill, open to performers and closed to kings

129.reading: Ay Andiran, war-winning lord of the great mountain of sweet jackfruit, where hill folk in low-eaved huts grow merry on toddy matured in bamboo and dance the kuravai in courtyards under the vengai: the elephants he gave to suppliants would match the stars only if the sky bloomed with stars everywhere, leaving no dark patch.
129.nuance: The hyperbole is hedged with a condition: the stars as they are fall short, so the sky must be imagined full. The kurinji scene of drinking and dancing is the patron's land, set out before his name.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron by the count of his gifts

130.reading: Ay of the bright jewelled ornament, does a young she-elephant in your land bear ten calves at a time? The noble elephants you gave gladly, without a grudging face, to those who come singing you and your mountain outnumber the spears the Kongar threw down when you drove them to the western sea.
130.nuance: The question is a joke that works as praise: so many elephants have been given that the herd must breed beyond nature. The comparison joins his giving to his war, counting gifts against an enemy's discarded spears.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron by the count of his gifts

131.reading: Did this lovely forest, so full of elephants, also sing the hill of Andiran, lord of the great cloud-resting mountain, who wears the vazhai flower and whose sword never fails?
131.nuance: The wit assumes the reader knows that singing Ay's hill earns elephants; the forest's wild herds are read as a bard's payment.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron through his reputation for giving elephants

132.reading: I thought of Ay only after others had thought of him first: may my heart sink, my tongue split and my ears silt up like a well in a deserted town; the Himalaya stands in the north, where the yak that grazed on fragrant naranthai grass drinks at the kuvalai pool and rests with its mate in the cool shade of the tagaram, and if Ay's clan did not stand in the south, this wide world would tip over.
132.nuance: The self-curse is the poet's apology for coming late to praise. The world-balance image sets a patron's family against the Himalaya as its counterweight, and the yak's ease in the north is drawn so fully that the south's single name has to outweigh a whole scene.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron's clan as the world's southern weight

comparisons.tenor: the poet's ears, deaf to praise

133.reading: Gentle dancer, you have only heard of his fame and never seen him; if you want to see him, go, your fragrant hair tossed by the mountain wind, moving lovely as a plumed peacock, to see Ay of the chariots, whose giving is like the rain.
133.nuance: The whole guide is a contrast of hearing and seeing: fame reaches the ear, but the gift is had only by going.

thinai_evidence.note: a performer directing another performer to a patron

134.reading: Ay is not a trader who buys virtue, saying that what is done in this life will pay in the next; his generous hand simply took the road that the worthy before him had travelled.
134.nuance: The poem names and rejects a motive for giving that was evidently current: giving as an investment in the next birth. What it puts in its place is not inner kindness but custom, the path the worthy have walked.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron's motive in giving

comparisons.tenor: one who gives for reward in the next life

135.reading: I climbed the narrow, painful path of the high tiger-haunted mountain, my bangled dancer following wearily, my small lute with strings like drawn gold held to my side, and came thinking only of your fame, lord of the mountain land where the elephant flees with her calf when she sees bards in the common ground: I want no elephants, horses or chariots; let bards and singers take those as their own, and may your days go on with the wealth you never call yours; I came only to see you.
135.nuance: The elephant that runs from bards is a joke about how freely Ay gives them away. By refusing the usual gifts the poet asks for the patron's presence, a bid that flatters by claiming a higher kind of want.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard addressing a patron about the gift he seeks

136.reading: Shall I call one enemy the lice and nits that cling in the seams of my many-patched rag, ribbed like the back of a lute? Another the hunger that wears down my many kin, flesh wasted and eyes brimming? Another the petty monkey-like robbers of the wooded slopes who swarm on me crying 'give what you have' without knowing my state? Trusting that Ay knows every enemy, praising your name, I crossed the sun-burnt wasteland: those who give to us give to others, and those who give to others give to themselves; I have said all this, so judge what suits you, give and send me off, and daily at Thuraiyur's ford we will eat your gift, praising you more times than its fine sands.
136.nuance: The catalogue of three enemies turns the bard's poverty into a war the patron is asked to win. The maxim in lines 20 and 21 is an argument, not a plea: a gift to the bard circulates, and in the end returns to the giver as fame.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard pressing a patron for the gift

comparisons.tenor: the number of the bard's praises

137.reading: I will no longer long for the three kings of the sea-bounded land with their roaring drums and herds of elephants; you are the one I know: in your land seed sown in the crowded pond does not die in drought but thrives like cane, flowers like eyes bloom even when summer dries the rain-water, and water like sapphire flows to the sea carrying the gold-like petals of the dark-stemmed vengai; lord of Nanjil of the red hills, ruler of the land of great rocks and small white falls, long may you live, and long live the father and mother who bore you.
137.nuance: The poet's renunciation of the three crowned kings is the measure of the small chief: a land that never fails in drought is a patron who never fails a bard. The blessing on the parents is a closing formula of praise.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a chief and his fertile land

comparisons.tenor: the seed that thrives in drought

138.reading: Bard in rags, with your small lute of strong-voiced strings, who crossed many paths full of cattle, left behind hills full of deer and swam many fords full of fish to come here: do not worry; your lord will never say 'come back later', for the husband of the lady with thick dark hair is like the great ear of grain in the wide field the parrots frequent, so who would know beforehand that you were coming?
138.nuance: The image of the grain-ear the parrots feed on makes the patron a crop open to any bird that comes, so no appointment is needed. The poem names no patron; the colophon gives Ay.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard directing another bard to a patron

comparisons.vehicle: கிளி மரீஇய வியன் புனத்து மரன் அணி பெருங்குரல்
comparisons.tenor: the patron, open to all who come

139.reading: Young men with loads pressing their shoulders and dancers with slim waists whose feet ache from the long climb are with me, and to live I speak the truth, not lies: lord of Nanjil of the high peaks, the plough-hill no one ploughs, descendant of men who never turned back, this is no time to wait for the ripe moment; the king has not stopped giving, and you do not fear death for your king, so if one day a hard battle comes like the earth heaving up, my suffering troupe may come to grief.
139.nuance: The bard's argument for speed is the patron's courage: a man who will die for his king may not be there tomorrow. The pun of the unploughed plough (உழாஅ நாஞ்சில்) praises the hill and its lord in one phrase.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard urging a patron to give now

140.reading: The lord of Nanjil with its wide-spreading jackfruit trees is surely a simpleton, red-tongued poets: when we asked for a little rice to go with the greens our bangled dancers had picked in the garden, he, knowing other kinds of due measure, weighed his own standing too and gave us a great elephant like a hill ringed by forest; is there any giving as unknowing as this? Do the great not keep watch over their own duty?
140.nuance: Praise disguised as blame: the patron is called foolish because he measured the gift by his own greatness rather than by the request. The closing question can be read as mock reproach (the great do not count the cost of their duty) or as a real one.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron through a gift far beyond the request

links.note: 121 tells Kari to give up the common gaze (பொது நோக்கு) and know each bard's rank (வரிசை); Kural 528 says a king who looks by rank (வரிசையா) rather than in common (பொதுநோக்கான்) draws many to live around him.
links.teaches: The Kural's two technical words for graded favour already stand in Kapilar's advice to a patron, so the Kural's rule for a king's kin was first argued by poets about how gifts should be ranked among themselves.

links.note: 121 says giving is easy and knowing due rank (வரிசை அறிதல்) is hard; 140 shows the lord of Nanjil, 'knowing rank' (வரிசை அறிதலின்), answering a request for rice with an elephant.
links.teaches: Read together, the two poems show that வரிசை cut both ways: 121 wants the patron to rank the recipient, 140 praises a patron who ranked by his own greatness and so overpaid, so the measure of a gift could be the giver's standing as well as the receiver's worth.

links.note: 121 asks the patron to stop treating all poets alike; Akananuru 152 praises Ay for giving freely to those who come whether skilled or not (வல்லினும் வல்லார் ஆயினும் சென்றோர்க்கு). On the plain reading the two ideals of giving are incompatible.
links.teaches: The akam poet borrows as an ornament exactly the indiscriminate giving that Kapilar argues against, so the ideal of the patron who gives to all was common fame, and 121 is a poet's dissent from it, not the standard view.

links.note: 123 praises Malayan of unfading fame (தொலையா நல்லிசை) at Mullur; Akananuru 209 names the Mullur king Kari whose fame does not pass (செல்லா நல்லிசை), who killed Ori and gave the Kolli hills to the Cheras.
links.teaches: The akam friend uses Kari's lasting fame as a fixed point to measure the heroine's beauty, which shows that the bards' praise of Kari had become a shared reference that akam poets could cite to measure something else entirely.

links.note: 126 calls Malaiyaman Kari lord of a land of palmyra groves (பெண்ணையம் படப்பை நாடு); Akananuru 35 names Kari of the long chariot, lord of Kovalur, and the great river Pennai (பெண்ணையம் பேரியாறு) at his ford.
links.teaches: The mother's lament in Akananuru 35 places her daughter's flight on the river of Kari's land, so a puram patron's territory supplies the akam poem's geography, and the shared பெண்ணையம் suggests that 126's phrase may name the river land rather than palms alone.

links.note: 128 says Ay's Pothiyil may be approached only by a dancing woman, while proud kings can hardly come near; Akananuru 322 compares the beloved, hard to win, to Pothiyil, hard to enter (புகலரும் பொதியில் போல).
links.teaches: The akam lover's simile takes its force from the puram boast: Pothiyil's inaccessibility was a known fact of Ay's power, and the akam poet turned a chief's closed hill into a measure of a woman's reserve.

links.note: 122 says nothing is Kari's own except his wife (நினது என இலை); 135 wishes Ay long life with the inheritance he does not grasp as his (எமதெனப் பற்றல் தேற்றா).
links.teaches: Two poets praising two different chiefs use the same figure of the owner who owns nothing, which marks it as a convention of the patron's praise rather than a fact about either man.

links.note: 127 sets Ay's emptied palace against the cities of drum-owning kings who eat alone, give nothing and lose their fame; Kural 1005 says those who neither give nor enjoy have nothing, though they hold crores.
links.teaches: The Kural's paradox that unshared wealth is poverty is shown in 127 from the other side, a bare palace that is rich in fame, so the pair gives both halves of one reckoning: the miser's full store is empty and the giver's empty hall is full.

links.note: 134 rejects as a merchant of virtue anyone who gives because what is done in this life serves the next; Naladiyar 95 tells the giver to give with an eye to the next world and this one (மறுமையும் இம்மையும் நோக்கி).
links.teaches: The Naladiyar's advice is the very motive the Sangam poet holds up for scorn, which shows that giving for the next birth was a live doctrine both poets knew, and that the older praise poetry judged it a lesser reason than custom and honour.

links.note: 134 says Ay does not give as a trade for the next world but because it is the path of the worthy; Kural 222 says giving is good even if there were no higher world.
links.teaches: Both refuse to found giving on reward hereafter, but they put different things in its place: the Kural a bare judgment that giving is good, the Purananuru the example of the worthy, so the same denial could rest either on principle or on custom.

links.note: 136 argues that those who give to the bard give to others and those who give to others give to themselves; Kural 221 says only giving to the destitute is giving and all else is a measured return (குறியெதிர்ப்பை).
links.teaches: The starving bard is exactly the Kural's destitute recipient, yet he argues that such giving does come back to the giver, so the Kural's line between true gift and loan was drawn against an older view in which even giving to the poor was defended by its return.

links.note: 139 urges the lord of Nanjil to give now, since he does not fear death for his king and a battle may come any day; Naladiyar 5 says not to hold back a gift thinking it can be given later, since Death drags all away.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar's general reason for giving now, the certainty of death, appears in 139 as a bard's practical argument tied to the warrior patron's own courage, which shows how the moralist's maxim was already a working plea in the bard's trade.

links.note: 123 counts Malayan's chariots as more than the raindrops on Mullur; 129 counts Ay's elephants against the stars of a sky with no dark patch.
links.teaches: Kapilar and Mudamosiyar measure gifts against a natural multitude, but Mudamosiyar adds a condition the real sky fails, so the second poet sharpens the formula by saying nature itself falls short of the count.

new_concepts.gloss: the gift a bard seeks from a patron, and the asking for it
new_concepts.label_source: the verses use the word: பரிசில் in 136 line 24 and 139 line 9; the colophons of 126, 135, 136, 139 and 140 use it in their thurai

new_concepts.gloss: a guide poem in which one performer directs another to a patron
new_concepts.label_source: the colophon thurai names it: விறலியாற்றுப்படை (133) and பாணாற்றுப் படை (138)

source_issues: 127: the colophon patron reads வேள் ஆய் அரண்டின், a misprint for ஆய் அண்டிரன் (the poem names ஆஅய், and 128 to 136 give அண்டிரன்).

139 and 140: the colophon patron is ஆய் அண்டிரன், but both poems address the lord of Nanjil (நாஞ்சில் பொருந, 139 line 8; நாஞ்சில் பொருநன், 140 line 1), the patron of 137 (நாஞ்சில் வள்ளுவன்); the patron field looks carried over from the Ay poems before them.
123 line 5: பயன்கிழு looks like a misprint for பயங்கெழு (fruitful), the epithet spelt so in 135 lines 7 and 18.
126 line 13: நிறகப் is a misprint for நிற்கப் (பரந்து இசை நிற்கப் பாடினன், he sang so that the fame spread and stood).
137 line 4: அரியு மோனே reads best as அறியுமோனே (the one I know); ர for ற.
138 line 3: மீளினம் is very likely மீனினம் (shoals of fish), matching ஆனினம் and மானினம் in lines 1 and 2; marked as fish.
134 line 2: ஆ அய் is ஆஅய் split by a stray space.
127: the colophon thurai கடைஇநிலை is the lengthened spelling of கடைநிலை; puram_thurai name normalised.

122, 124, 126: the review's line table says sangamtamil.com lacks our opening line(s) (122 line 1; 124 lines 1-2; 126 line 1, and has two lines we lack). 122 line 1 and 124 lines 1-2 carry sense the following lines complete, so all our lines are marked; 126's opening was not compared against the site, as the brief forbids using it, and is marked as it stands.
137 line 1 is flagged as repeated in 270 line 2; it is a formula for the crowned kings' drums and elephants, not a copying error.
